The Story of Sanatkumar Chakravarti

Bowing to the Arhats, Siddhas, Acharyas, Upadhyayas, and Sadhus — bestowers of heaven and liberation — I write the story of the fourth Sanatkumar Chakravarti, who illuminated the path of right conduct.

In the land of Bharat, within the region called Anantvirya, there stood a city named Vitshok. Its king was Anantvirya, and his queen was Sita. Their son, Sanatkumar, was the fruit of their great merit. He became a Chakravarti — a universal emperor. Among those who held right faith, he stood foremost. He had brought all six divisions of the earth under his dominion.

The sages described the measure of his wealth thus: nine treasures, fourteen jewels, eighty-four lakhs of elephants, as many chariots, eighteen crores of horses, eighty-four crores of valiant warriors, ninety-six crores of grain-filled villages, ninety-six thousand beautiful women, and thirty-two thousand great kings ever ready in his service. Celestial beings and Vidyadharas attended upon him. He was extraordinarily handsome and supremely fortunate. His faith in the Jain dharma was unwavering. He performed his daily and occasional rituals with devotion, never allowing any obstacle to interrupt them. He governed his vast empire with wisdom and passed his days in contentment.

One day, the Indra of Saudharma heaven was praising the beauty of mortal men in his celestial court. A witty god asked him, "Lord, this beauty you praise so lavishly — does any man in Bharat truly possess such beauty, or is this mere flattery?" Indra replied, "Even now there is a man in Bharat whose beauty neither humans nor gods can match. His name is Sanatkumar Chakravarti."

Hearing Indra praise a beauty rare even among gods, two deities named Manimal and Ratchul could not contain their longing. They descended in disguise from heaven to Bharat and came upon the Chakravarti while he was bathing. Even stripped of his royal garments and ornaments, his form was the fairest in all three worlds. They had to nod in agreement — his beauty was exactly as Indra had described, truly beyond the reach of gods.

After witnessing his form, the two gods returned to heaven and reported what they had seen. Their account only deepened the wonder of the celestial court. But Sanatkumar himself cared nothing for the praise of his beauty. His mind was set upon higher things.

One day, while the Chakravarti sat in his court, a messenger arrived with news that troubled him deeply. He learned that despite all his power, wealth, and beauty, there were sorrows that no empire could conquer — old age, sickness, and death. The thought took root in his heart like a seed in fertile soil. He began to reflect: "What use is this body, however beautiful, if it must decay? What use is this empire if it cannot shield me from suffering?"

Sanatkumar resolved to renounce his throne. He summoned his ministers and his family and declared his intention. They were dismayed and pleaded with him to reconsider. "You are young," they said. "You are the lord of the entire earth. Enjoy your kingdom now; take up renunciation in your old age." But Sanatkumar replied, "Death does not wait for old age. The wise renounce while they still have the strength to do so."

With steadfast resolve, he placed the burden of the empire upon his heir and left his palace. He took initiation as a Jain monk under the guidance of a great Acharya. As a monk, he observed the most rigorous vows — perfect non-violence, absolute truthfulness, complete non-possession. He bore every hardship with equanimity: heat and cold, hunger and thirst, praise and blame.

His conduct was so pure that even the gods came to witness it. They marvelled that a man who had possessed every pleasure the world can offer had abandoned it all for the sake of the soul's liberation. His right conduct became a beacon, inspiring thousands to walk the path of dharma.

In time, through the fire of deep meditation, Sanatkumar destroyed all his destructive karmas and attained keval jnan — the supreme, infinite knowledge. He spent the remainder of his life as a wandering teacher, guiding countless souls toward liberation. At the end of his life, he attained moksha — the eternal, blissful state beyond all rebirth.

The story of Sanatkumar Chakravarti teaches us that true greatness lies not in beauty, wealth, or power, but in the willingness to renounce them all for the sake of the soul. Right conduct, lived with unwavering dedication, is the straight path to liberation.
